notes.meaning: Jacob, also called Israel, had twelve sons who became the founding fathers of the twelve tribes of Israel. Their names are listed together to show the whole covenant family before the writer focuses closely on the tribe of Judah. Even though several of these brothers had serious faults, God chose their families by his own grace to be his special people.

Judah is listed first among the tribes because the royal ruler and the Messiah were promised to come from his family line. Judah had three sons with a Canaanite woman named Bath-shua. His oldest son, Er, was wicked in the Lord's sight, so the Lord brought an early death upon him.

Judah also had twin sons named Perez and Zerah through his daughter-in-law Tamar, giving him five sons in total. Perez became the ancestor through whom the royal family line of King David would continue. This shows how God works out his holy plans even through painful and broken family situations.

Perez had two sons named Hezron and Hamul. Hezron is especially important in the Bible because he stands in the direct ancestral line leading to King David. Hamul also started a family clan in Israel, though little else is recorded about him.

Zerah's family line included five notable men: Zimri, Ethan, Heman, Calcol, and Dara. Ethan and Heman were widely renowned in ancient times for their wisdom and musical skill. King Solomon was later praised by being called even wiser than these famous brothers.

Achar was a descendant of Zerah through Carmi and is called Achan in the book of Joshua. He brought great trouble on the whole nation of Israel by stealing spoils from Jericho that were devoted completely to God. The name Achar means 'troubler,' which reminds readers of the national disaster caused by his unfaithfulness.

Ethan had a son named Azariah. The Bible gives no further details about his life or deeds, but his name is preserved to honor his family branch. Even lesser-known individuals had a valued place in the records of God's people.

Hezron had three sons named Jerahmeel, Ram, and Caleb, who is also called Chelubai. Each of these three sons founded a major branch within the tribe of Judah. The writer follows the line of Ram first because it leads directly to King David.

These verses trace the royal family tree from Ram down through six generations to Jesse. Nahshon, the son of Amminadab, served as the chief prince of the tribe of Judah during the wilderness journey from Egypt. This exact family line is recorded later in the book of Ruth and in the New Testament as the family tree of Jesus Christ.

Jesse is recorded here as having seven sons, with David listed as the seventh and youngest. Earlier historical passages mention that Jesse had eight sons when Samuel visited his home. One of the brothers likely died young without leaving any children, so his name was not included in this formal family registry.

David had two sisters, Zeruiah and Abigail, whose sons became powerful warriors in his kingdom. Zeruiah was the mother of Abishai, Joab, and Asahel, who were top commanders in David's army. Abigail was the mother of Amasa, whose father was Jether the Ishmaelite.

Caleb the son of Hezron had sons named Jesher, Shobab, and Ardon through his wife Azubah. This Caleb is an earlier figure and not the same man as Caleb son of Jephunneh, the famous spy who explored the Promised Land. The record preserves the names of these sons to show how Caleb's household grew.

After Azubah died, Caleb married Ephrath, and she gave birth to a son named Hur. Hur became the father of Uri, and Uri was the father of Bezalel. Bezalel was the master craftsman whom God filled with his Spirit to design and build the holy tabernacle.

When Hezron was sixty years old, he married the daughter of Machir from the tribe of Manasseh, and she gave birth to Segub. Segub was the father of Jair, a bold leader who controlled twenty-three towns in the region of Gilead. This marriage created a strong family bridge between the tribes of Judah and Manasseh.

The neighboring kingdoms of Geshur and Aram later captured the towns of Jair, along with the city of Kenath and its sixty villages. All these people were counted among the descendants of Machir, the father of Gilead. Jair had cast his lot with his mother's family, so his lands were reckoned with theirs.

Hezron died in Caleb-ephrathah, a location connected with Bethlehem that combined the names of Caleb and his wife. After Hezron's death, his wife Abijah gave birth to a son named Ashhur. Ashhur became the founder and principal leader of the town of Tekoa in Judah.

Jerahmeel was Hezron's firstborn son, and his first wife bore him five sons: Ram, Bunah, Oren, Ozem, and Ahijah. Jerahmeel also had a second wife named Atarah, who became the mother of Onam. These details map out the early branches of the Jerahmeelite clan.

Ram, the firstborn son of Jerahmeel, had three sons named Maaz, Jamin, and Eker. Jerahmeel's other son Onam had two sons named Shammai and Jada. Listing these side branches of Judah helped the returning exiles know their full family heritage.
